html:
SMTO-AUT-0010 — The service refused or withdrew SMTO's access

GUID: 9d9f1c52-3728-5b06-8037-fdfc43608788
Slug: auth-authorization-denied
Domain: AUT · Subsystem: auth-broker

What happened

  • The connected service didn't give SMTO the access it asked for, or no longer accepts access it gave before. This happens when Deny is chosen on the sign-in page or SMTO's access is removed from the account.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Find out which account should be used. If the service says an administrator must approve the app, ask that administrator to approve it first. Until the right account approves, the service keeps refusing SMTO's request.
  2. If the Task was making a change, such as sending a message, check the service to see whether it already happened. SMTO won't repeat an action on its own when it can't be sure what happened earlier.
  3. If the change still needs doing, ask SMTO in the conversation to try the step again. Select Open authorization page, sign in with that account, and allow the access. A fresh approval replaces the access that was refused or withdrawn.

What success looks like

  • The sign-in page says Authorization complete, and the Task continues without this error.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who set up this connection. If you no longer want SMTO to use this service, select Stop on the Task instead of approving access.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The OAuth provider rejected the grant: the authorization callback carried an error (for example access_denied), or the token endpoint answered access_denied or invalid_grant for the saved grant.

What this means

  • The provider returned access_denied, invalid_grant or an authorization callback error; the response rejects the current grant rather than proving a password defect. Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.

Why this can happen

  • The provider returned access_denied, invalid_grant or an authorization callback error; the response rejects the current grant rather than proving a password defect.

How to diagnose it

  • Compare consent outcome with refresh rejection; confirm whether the intended user still wants this access.

How to fix it

  • Check the provider's consent and audit records for this user and client (denied consent, an admin-consent requirement, revoked app access or an expired refresh grant), then restart authorization so fresh consent is recorded. Do not reuse old authorization codes or automatically repeat an operation whose remote effect is unknown.
  • Review provider consent and reconnect the saved connection if the intended access is still required.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the reported condition and check delivery evidence before starting another operation.

How to verify the fix

  • Fresh intended consent or a valid existing grant establishes the required authorization.

What not to do

  • Do not expose passwords, access tokens, authorization codes or SMTP authentication payloads.
  • Do not automatically repeat an operation whose remote effect is unknown.

Technical notes

  • Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
